#8719. How Yonatan Katz Cracked the Boulder Nobody Could Solve at the World Climbing Series

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Climbing is what happens when you take a gym rat’s obsession with grip strength, remove the floor, and let gravity do its thing. There’s no bench to lie on, no belt to tighten, and no place to hide a weak link. You have to get your body up a wall using holds that sometimes look so bleak the edge of a credit card looks like it might offer more purchase. And if you screw up, you better hope your rope is knotted correctly.

That was on full display at the World Climbing Series bouldering finale in Salt Lake City, October 16-18. In the men’s final, Israel’s Yonatan Katz won gold on only his second start in the senior international series. He went into the final problem behind Britain’s Maximillian Milne and came out the winner after pulling off a move nobody else in the final had managed.

Here’s how it happened. The last boulder was a nasty coordination problem. Before Katz stepped up, the other finalists who had attempted it hadn’t even reached the scoring zone, a designated hold partway up the route. On his fourth try, Katz got past the zone and reached the top. He finished with 69.7 points. Milne couldn’t answer on his turn and took silver with 59.7. Japan’s Rei Kawamata was third with 54.2. For a sport that looks, to outsiders, like a bunch of people climbing a wall, there was a hell of a lot of drama hanging off those holds.

The women’s final the next day had its own story. France’s Oriane Bertone won with 84.6 points after being the only finalist to complete the first boulder. Britain’s Erin McNeice finished second with 69.7, barely ahead of Japan’s Mao Nakamura at 69.6. McNeice didn’t win that night, but she won the season-long Boulder title. She’d opened the series in 11th place and followed it with a gold and four silvers.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Sorato Anraku had already locked up the men’s overall championship after winning five of the six bouldering events. Then he failed to advance from qualification in Salt Lake City. Even the guy who dominated the season can get humbled by a fresh set of plastic holds. If bodybuilding judges replaced their comparison rounds with problems that changed every week, we’d see a few interesting faces backstage.

Bouldering is done on relatively short walls with thick mats instead of ropes. The athlete has to solve a sequence of moves, reach designated holds, and control the top. Strength matters, obviously. So does the ability to position your hips, push through your feet, generate momentum, and decide what to do before your forearms turn into concrete. Some moves are slow and surgical. Others look like a gymnast being thrown into a hardware store. The best climbers aren’t simply pulling themselves upward. They’re figuring out how to make the least-wasteful movement possible under pressure.

There’s a lesson in there for anybody who trains. A giant back and a crushing handshake don’t automatically make you good at something that requires timing, balance, and technical skill. Nor does being smaller make you weak. Climbing exposes the difference between owning strength and knowing how to use it. And if you’re tempted to try it, start with an introductory session, not an advanced overhang and a heroic declaration. A 2026 review of 45 climbing-injury studies found frequent problems involving fingers, hands, shoulders, and ankles. Those little finger pulleys weren’t designed to absorb your entire ego on day one.

I like sports that punish bullshit. Climbing is high on that list. There’s no score for looking intimidating while you chalk your hands, and no bonus for explaining how strong you’d be if the holds were bigger. Katz won because he solved a problem that had stopped the others. McNeice took the season because she kept delivering. The wall doesn’t care about your résumé, your physique, or your excuses. It only cares whether you can get to the top.

#8715. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Mr. Money Mustache April 7, 2023, 4:27 pm

Good point Stephanie – I believe that part is coming soon, as the first batch of apartments open up and are ready for rent (right now you are only signing up for the waiting list rather than an actual apartment).

Since I was there and asked the same question in person, the answer is basically “market rate” – in other words, when a new apartment goes up for rent, the builders typically conduct a price survey of what would be a competitive price at that moment, and then they start advertising at that price.

Just like any other supply and demand sensitive thing, these prices will then fluctuate based on the demand level until you lock it in with a lease. During my tour, it was a hot time for rentals in prosperous Tempe so the rent was around $2.50 per square foot per month, or a little under $2k for a large 1-bedroom apartment.

Note that at Culdesac you get a few extra perks included in that rent: internet access that works across the whole 17 acre campus, gym, pool, and unlimited transit pass along with credits for bike and carshare as well.

Since the idea is to go car-free while living there, you can possibly subtract about $800/month that most people spend on car ownership, from your total cost of living.

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

#8714. The Glute Training Guide for a Stronger and More Powerful Posterior

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Not every muscle gets immortalized in a rap song, but the glutes do more than look good in pants. Beyond the vanity benefits, the glutes help you do fun things in and out of the gym.

Although the gluteus maximus gets all the attention, the gluteus medius and minimus provide the stability that lets the glute max do its job better. That’s why it’s important to focus on all three, not just one.

Compound lifts hit them hard and heavy, but isolation exercises are necessary to train all glute functions and muscles. You can also load them in different ways: from a lengthened position (think RDL) and from a shortened position (think Hip Thrust).

Understanding those differences, rather than choosing sides in the great squat-versus-hip-thrust debate, is key to better glute training.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gQnMPHoDGEc

Each glute muscle has a different role, and understanding them will help you train them more effectively.

It’s the largest and most superficial of the three muscles, and it’s responsible for much of your backside’s size and shape. Although it’s best known for hip extension and external rotation, some lower fibers can assist with hip adduction depending on hip position, while the upper fibers assist with hip abduction.

The gluteus medius sits on the lateral side of your pelvis, partly beneath the gluteus maximus. Its primary job is hip abduction, but it also helps stabilize the pelvis. It also has different muscle fibers that perform different jobs. The anterior fibers assist with hip internal rotation, while the posterior fibers can contribute to external rotation.

The gluteus minimus is the smallest and deepest of the three, sitting underneath the glute medius. It assists with hip abduction and internal rotation while helping control the femur’s position within the hip joint. It also works with the glute medius to stabilize the pelvis when one foot leaves the ground.

The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that allows your hips to flex, extend, abduct, adduct, and rotate. But not everyone’s ball-and-socket joint is built the same way.

The depth and orientation of your hip socket, the angle of your femoral neck, and how much your femur rotates forward or backward vary from person to person. These structural differences influence exercise selection and positions.

Some squat with a narrow stance and toes pointed forward, while others go wider with toes pointed out. Your hip anatomy, mobility, strength, and limb length all influence what position works best for you. Adjusting your stance, foot position, and range of motion can help you find positions that load the glutes effectively and work with your anatomy.

Your glutes are among the body’s most powerful muscles, and paying attention to your backside pays off in more ways than one.

Glutes give you the horsepower to do the things you enjoy, from squatting to sprinting to other daily activities. The stronger they are, the more force they can produce, especially when you pair that strength with power training.

In many unilateral movements like walking, running, walking upstairs, and single-leg RDLs, smaller glute muscles control your lower-body position. Weakness can show up in a loss of balance, excessive wobbling in a single-leg stance, or your knee caving inward during squats and deadlifts. You don’t want any of that.

Your hips, knees, and lower back are teammates, and when one struggles, another may compensate. Weak glute med and glute min can cause knee valgus, which your knee ligaments don’t like. Weak hip extension strength or limited hip mobility forces the lower back to do a job it’s not designed for. Training the glutes for strength and mobility prevents this.

Almost every powerful lower-body movement involves the glutes.

During sprinting, the gluteus maximus drives powerful hip extension. When you cut, land, or change direction, all three glute muscles help control the hip and pelvis as your body absorbs and redirects force. The glutes also contribute to rotational movements, such as swinging a bat, throwing a punch, and a golf swing. Their ability to produce force and rotate helps link lower-body movement to upper-body power.

Here’s what your glutes need to grow bigger and stronger.

Compound exercises such as barbell squats, Romanian deadlifts, and barbell hip thrusts let the glutes produce force alongside the quads, hamstrings, and adductors, making them an excellent foundation for building strength and muscle.

Deep squats, front-foot elevated split squats, and deficit reverse lunges put a loaded stretch where you need it most. Because the hips are flexed and the glutes are lengthened, they can build greater muscle. Bonus points for using a controlled lowering phase.

Barbell hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickback variations emphasize hip extension as the glutes approach their shortened position, given their smaller range of motion.

Neither approach is better, but both can help develop the glutes.

Hip abduction machines, lateral band walks, and side-lying hip raises train the gluteus medius, minimus, and the upper fibers of the gluteus maximus. These improve hip stability, allowing the glute max to work more effectively.

Seated band hip internal rotation, cable hip external rotation, and seated 90/90 hip rotations rotate the thigh within the hip joint while keeping the pelvis and lower back locked in. Rotational training supports hip stability, health, and more complete lower-body development.

The dreaded Bulgarian split squats, single-leg RDL’s, and step-ups train one leg at a time, improving hip stability. Unilateral exercises challenge the glutes to produce force and stabilize the pelvis, improving balance while strengthening imbalances between sides.

You don’t need 15 different glute exercises, but the right combination of movements that cover their various functions without turning every leg day into a marathon.

Start With Compound Bilateral And Unilateral Lifts

Compound lower-body lifts are the foundation of glute training because they let you go hard and heavy while other muscles join the party. But here’s an important distinction: Many compound lifts don’t isolate the glutes.

Compound lifts build strength and muscle, but moving more total weight doesn’t always mean the glutes get all the love. Squat depth, torso angle, hip position, and exercise technique influence how much work the glutes perform.

You need more than one type of hip-extension exercise because different movements challenge the glutes at different muscle lengths. Romanian deadlifts, full-range-of-motion squats, and front-foot elevated split squats load the glutes when they’re lengthened, while hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickbacks emphasize tension closer to full hip extension, when the glutes are shorter.

Both can build size and strength, and each offers something the other doesn’t.

Don’t get caught up in the Team Squat versus Team Hip Thrust debate. Include exercises that challenge the glutes at both longer and shorter lengths, use a full range of motion you can control, and overload when you can.

Debates don’t build muscle. Training does.

Compound exercises train the glute med and mini, but direct hip-abduction exercises give them extra attention. When they’re stronger, your glute max can go to work unencumbered.

Broad jumps, sled pushes, hill sprints, and lateral bounds powerfully train the glutes and fire up your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which drive many of your gains. These exercises are great if you want your strength to carry over to athletic activities.

Your glutes can only work within the ranges your hips can access and control. Include half-kneeling hip flexor stretches with a posterior pelvic tilt, adductor rockbacks, 90/90 hip rotations, and prying squats in your warm-up to prepare for the work ahead.

The trick to training your glutes well is balancing heavy lifting, muscle-building work, and stability exercises while giving your backside enough time to recover. Here’s how to make it work.

Perform lower-body compound exercises, both bilateral and unilateral, with challenging weights. Maintain your technique and rest two to three minutes, or longer, between sets. Focus on progressive overload without sacrificing range of motion.

Again, use compound lower-body exercises that hit both lengthened and shortened positions, with a controlled eccentric contraction and full range of motion, training close to technical failure. Although muscle growth can happen across a wider rep range, this range balances load, effort, and fatigue.

Perform power movements early in your workout when you’re fresh, focus on maximum movement speed and quality, and rest 2 minutes or longer when needed to maintain explosiveness.

Hip abduction machines, cable abductions, and side-lying variations allow you to focus on the smaller glute muscles. Use controlled reps, avoid momentum, and progress the load.

Single-leg RDLs, step-ups, and Bulgarian split squats build strength while challenging stability. Only progress as your strength and balance improve.

Your weekly training volume should include all glute-focused exercises. Use the following table as a guideline, not a rule set in stone.

Some exercises train several qualities at once. A Bulgarian split squat challenges glute strength, muscle growth, and stability, but you don’t count the same set three times. Assign each set to its primary programming purpose (muscle/stability) when using the table.

For most lifters, two to three sessions per week is a good starting point.

Beginners can split their weekly work into two sessions, while intermediate lifters can use two or three. Experienced lifters focused on glute development will benefit from spreading the work over three sessions to maintain training quality.

Training your glutes isn’t rocket science, but you can make it harder than it needs to be. Here’s what to watch for and how to fix it.

Hip thrusts and bridge variations are excellent for building the glutes from the shortened position, but making them your only option misses opportunities to challenge the muscles at longer lengths and train hip abduction and stability.

The fix: Combine hip thrusts with RDLs, squats, split squats, and direct hip abduction exercises to cover more of the glutes’ functions.

It’s tempting to focus on exercises where you can really feel the squeeze, but muscle growth isn’t determined by how hard you can contract your glutes at lockout. RDLs, deep squats, and front-foot-elevated split squats challenge the glutes at longer muscle lengths, providing a different training stimulus.

The fix: Include at least one exercise that loads the glutes during greater hip flexion.

When chasing the squeeze or extra ROM in a hip thrust, deadlift, or RDL variation, some lifters extend their lower back instead of their glutes. Overarching your back at the top creates movement that doesn’t originate in the hips and shifts the focus away from where it belongs.

The fix: Keep your ribs over your hips, extend through your hips, and stop when you reach lockout.

The gluteus maximus gets the glory, but the smaller glute muscles help stabilize your pelvis, support the ball-and-socket movement, and produce hip abduction. Relying on compound lower-body exercises may leave these muscles undertrained.

The fix: Include band, cable, or machine hip abduction variations to give these smaller muscles the attention they deserve.

There’s one camp that says all you need for glutes is squats. Another camp says hip thrusts are all you need. Opinions run wild, so let’s separate fact from fiction.

Squats are fantastic for building glutes from a lengthened position, but the glutes need more than that, as they don’t challenge every glute function.

The truth: No one doubts squats are great for glutes, but training from a shortened position and direct hip-abduction exercises provide a different stimulus that can enhance muscle development.

Doing a set of hip thrusts tells you you’re engaging your glutes, but just because you “feel” it more doesn’t mean hip thrusts are better than squats for building muscle. Greater muscle activation during an exercise doesn’t necessarily translate into greater long-term muscle growth.

The truth: Research comparing hip thrusts and squats shows both build the glutes effectively, despite their different mechanics. For some, it comes down to personal preference.

Influencers with great glutes will scream from the rooftops that you can isolate and build an upper-glute shelf and a better lower-glute hamstring tie-in. But here’s some fact behind that fiction: The glute maximus has different fiber orientations that contribute to hip extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation.

The truth: Certain exercises and hip positions can shift the emphasis toward different glute regions, but you cannot turn off one area while training another. This is similar to what I explored in the upper- and lower-ab training myth.

If you walk up the stairs or sit down in slow motion after glute day, you might assume you’ve had the greatest glute workout ever. Hold your jeans.

The truth: Extreme muscle soreness usually signals a new training stimulus or heavy eccentric loading, and it isn’t a reliable measure of muscle gain.

Adjust the loads, sets, reps, and exercise variations to match your experience and recovery. Perform them as standalone sessions or fit them into your existing program.

Rest periods: Rest two to three minutes after each superset and 90 seconds between exercises.

Progressive overload: When you reach the upper end of a rep range with clean technique, increase the load slightly.

Manage weekly volume: The full-body workout includes nine glute-focused resistance sets, while the lower-body workout includes 11. Keep that in mind when combining these into your current routine or performing both in the same week.

People rap about and admire the glutes, but they’re the engine that makes the body roar in and out of the gym.

Building stronger, more muscular glutes takes more than hip thrusts and band booty burners. Train the glute max through all its functions, give the med and mini some love, and combine exercises that challenge your backside in lengthened and shortened positions. Include unilateral training, progressive overload, and adequate rest and recovery, and your jeans will thank you.

One last thing. Turn around and admire your handy work.

Liam Fitzgerald, a popular online coach and fitness influencer has passed away at just 29 years of age after injuries sustained during a fatal motorcycle accident. Tributes have poured in for the star, and his family have hailed him as an inspirational figure.

Fitzgerald, who was born in Evansville, Wisconsin, and was a social media influencer and OnlyFans creator, died on October 30, per announcement by his girlfriend Jamie Lyn Rinaldi. “It is with the heaviest heart that I share the devastating news that Liam passed away following a motorcycle accident on October 30th at approximately 2 AM,” she wrote via Instagram. “He suffered severe injuries, and despite the efforts of those who tried desperately to save him, they were unable to bring him back. There are no words to describe the heartbreak of this loss.”

Fitzgerald was an athlete before becoming an influencer and after a move to Washington state, his teenage years were highly active. Fitzgerald played football as a quarterback for the Camas Papermakers, skateboarded, and developed a love of working out. He later relocated to Arizona and finally settled in Miami, Florida, where he built an Instagram base of more than one million followers by sharing his fitness, fashion, and lifestyle advice.

Fitzgerald also collaborated with well known brands such as YoungLA, who posted a tribute to the star via its official Instagram account. “He brought an incredible energy, joy, and excitement to every shoot, making every moment that much more special,” read the statement. “His presence will be deeply missed, and we are grateful to have had the opportunity to work alongside him.”

The influencer’s family has also spoken about Fitzgerald’s struggles with alcohol. “This is shared in the hope that his story reaches someone who needs it,” read a statement. “He wasn’t perfect and never pretended to be. But he always strived to grow and do better. He had dreams, ambitions, and so much more life to live. He had just turned 29. So many places to see, memories to make, and people to love. His life was tragically cut short in a motorcycle accident, leaving behind a heartbreak that words will never be able to describe.”

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

You'll need 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. Check your current balances across:

Decide your primary transfer source before you need the points. If you're using Capital One, initiate the transfer 5–7 days before you want to book to give yourself buffer time.

If you don't have a Privilege Club account, create one at qatarairways.com/privilege-club — it's free and takes minutes. Once you have your account number, you can link it as a transfer destination in your Citi, Capital One, or Marriott account.

Once you've confirmed availability and are ready to book, log into your credit card rewards portal and initiate the transfer to your Qatar Privilege Club account number. For Citi, this will post instantly. For Capital One, monitor your Avios balance over the next 2–5 days.

Return to qatarairways.com, log into your Privilege Club account, and book the award using your Avios balance. Have your passport and payment method ready for the taxes and fees. Confirm the aircraft type one final time at booking to ensure you're on a QSuites-equipped aircraft.

If you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Also try ±3 days on either side of your target dates — availability patterns are uneven. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

British Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Let's build a real booking so the numbers stop being abstract.

The Route: New York JFK → Doha DOH on Qatar Airways, Boeing 777-300ER, QSuites Business Class.

Cash Price: A one-way QSuites ticket on this route runs roughly $5,000–$8,000 depending on timing and booking window. For a couple, you're looking at $10,000–$16,000 in cash — a number that probably makes the FI-minded reader physically uncomfortable.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

You arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

Dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

This is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.

#8697. How Kimi Antonelli Trains His Brain for Peak Speed—and an F1 Record

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

It’s official, 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli has secured his spot as the youngest F1 Champion in history after just two seasons, but while the dedicated Mercedes driver has been relentless on the track, the speedy Italian has also stayed active outside of his car. Here’s why the history maker’s appetite for adventure is the reason that he never stays still, and how a smart approach to staying active benefits both body and mind.

Kimi Antonelli’s third place in Mexico City on November 1 meant that he’d earned enough points to stave off all other drivers to complete the season as champion, but this overnight success is the result of a mature approach to staying sharp. “I try to do things that keep me active, but won’t tire me out,” explained Antonelli during a recent and telling interview with GQ. “It’s all a way to release mental stress, to just relax and enjoy. I try to do these activities as much as possible because in sports, the mental [part] is basically what does everything.”

The activities that Antonelli spoke of include race related training such as simulators, go-karts, and operating remote controlled cars, but he’s also a keen proponent of padel. Not only has the young upstart played against fellow Mercedes drivers like George Russell, but he’s even been known to stroke the ball from the deck of a super yacht from time to time.

Antonelli’s fuel for dominating F1 was on show early, as he transitioned from Formula 2 and continued his approach to “hard” training, sharing that a day of working out included “An early morning swim, neck training at lunch, and an afternoon bike ride.”

The inspirational Italian is also hot with the hoops, and in a recent Instagram Reel revealed that he can make a basket from an impressive distance, all while standing on one leg!

While Antonelli’s love of fun activities helps him keep a positive mindset as he works towards pole position, science has also shown that becoming skilled in a variety of sporting activities can only help with his day job. Activities such as shooting baskets, stroking the Padel ball, and other loves such as surfing, no doubt boost his reaction times. In fact, a scientific study in 2023 confirmed that reaction training (they used flashing lights as the stimuli) induced beneficial effects on physiological and cognitive performance.

At just 20 years of age, Kimi Antonelli has the world at his highly successful feet. So, what’s next? “Right now, my main goal is to give everything to F1, but in my normal life, I want to be successful, too,” he revealed to GQ. “I want to be efficient, and in 20 to 30 years’ time, when I won’t be racing anymore, I want to still do something that keeps me active. Because once you finish, it’s easy to do nothing after working hard for so many years. I want to be successful outside of racing.”

With an attitude like Antonelli’s, the journey is far from over.

#8694. Frugal Man Buys $52,000 Car – Why??

As I type this, I’m jumping through the various hoops involved in buying a 2023 Tesla Model Y, a rather expensive, luxury “crossover” that is absolutely loaded to the gills with excess: all wheel drive, faster acceleration than a Lamborghini, enough space for seven people and enough computer gadgetry to function as a small Google data center.

Update: Looking for the ongoing tracker page? It’s here at “The Model Y Experiment“

The total net cost of this thing to me after all the taxes and tax credits* will be about $52,000, which is just a stunning amount higher than the Honda van it is replacing. That old classic cost me $4500 when I bought it off of Craigslist twelve years ago, and it had served me dutifully until just last month, crisscrossing the mountains and deserts of this country and also helping to rebuild a considerable swath of houses in my neighborhood.

I’m supposed to be a frugality-oriented financial blogger, and I’m also known for hating car culture – I think most people use cars about ten times more often than they need to, and most people drive cars they can’t afford. So why the hell am I buying a new one?

From those first three paragraphs, you can see I’m feeling plenty of self-mockery and ridicule over this new purchase. If you’re also a naturally frugal person, you can surely relate to the thoughts and you probably also agree with me that I’m off my rocker.

And indeed, I’m still on-board with frugality and healthy self mockery. After all, it was this overall life philosophy that earned me an early retirement 18 years ago, which provides all of the glorious freedom I enjoy now.

It was also the philosophy that allowed me to procrastinate on buying this expensive car for the last four years, even as countless people both close to me and out on the Internet egged me on and told me I should just loosen up and treat myself.

But there’s a classic slogan that applies to many areas of life, and it is something I like to dig up and ponder every now and then:

How does that piece of wisdom apply to frugal living and enjoying a long life of early retirement?

A quick story from a recent run to the grocery store will explain:

I was standing there in the bakery aisle, hoping to restock with a loaf of Dave’s Killer Bread for the next day’s breakfast with some visiting friends. But since this was in a standard grocery store rather than the Costco where I usually shop, the damned stuff was priced at an eye-watering $6.99 per loaf (instead the $4.50 or so I’m accustomed to paying, and even at the bulk store this stuff is about double the price of normal bread).

“WHO THE HELL DO YOU THINK YOU ARE, TRYING TO SELL BREAD FOR SEVEN BUCKS!!!”

Then I went through a whole mental battle of what I call Grocery Shopping With Your Middle Finger:

“Hmm I wonder if any of the other competing brands are any good?”

“What else is a good substitute for bread for this breakfast?”

And then thankfully, after exhausting all other mental options, I settled on the correct one:

“Because you are never going to wake up in the future and look at your bank account and think, shit, if only I had an extra $2.49 in there I would be a happier person.”

That night, I came home from the store and shared this funny tale with one of my guests. He understood perfectly because he too had earned his own retirement through a lifetime of grinding in tough jobs and disciplined frugality. And despite the fact that he has a net worth several times higher than mine, he admitted that he faces exactly the same mental battles over splurging on himself.

This same friend gives freely to charitable causes, has supported a local school for decades, and is always the first one to pull out the checkbook if a friend has hit hard times or is looking for a trusted business investor.

But he still has trouble bringing himself to take an Uber to the airport instead of riding the bus which takes an hour longer.

We both realized that we were being too cheap with ourselves, and we needed to work on it. And we came up with a set of three ideas that should hopefully work together to help us have more fun with our life savings, while we are still alive:

Principle #1: The Minimum Spending Budget:

Suppose you’ve done well over the years and amassed a pile of productive investments worth about two million dollars. Yes, this is a lot of money for most people, and that is the point: this hypothetical person truly has it made.

But as it turns out, most Mustachians I know with this level of wealth are still living very efficient lives, usually with a spending level of under $40,000 per year. On top of that, they typically live in a mortgage-free house and still have various forms of side income from a small business or two.

The 4% rule tells us that this person should be fairly safe spending up to about $80,000 per year from that cozy nest egg, even if they never earn any other money.

If this person wanted to be ridiculously conservative and set the spending rate at 3%, that still leaves about $60,000 of fun money every single year.. Plus, again, any side income, future inheritances, and social security income only add to the surplus.

Thus, a reasonable minimum spending level for this person might be $60,000 per year.

And in most cases, they know this, but still go right on living on $40k or less and claim they have everything they could ever want.

But if you watch carefully you’ll still catch them firing up the middle finger at things like $6.99 Dave’s bread or the $14.00 Cabernet at the restaurant or driving around in a gas guzzler even when they would prefer to have a proper, modern electric car.

And whenever these people do get extra money, their first instinct is to stash it away on top of the already-too-big pile.  In diagram form, their money flow looks like this:

Note that while this person is great at accumulating money through that big red arrow firing money back into the ‘stash, their “fun stuff” arrow appears quite flaccid and withered.

Principle #2 – the Dedicated Money Wasting Account

Lifelong habits are hard to break, and it’s sometimes hard to “waste” your own hard-earned money on things that seem frivolous, even when you know intellectually that you have way more money than you’ll ever spend.

But have you ever noticed that if you are spending somebody else’s money, preferably an anonymous corporation, it feels different?

For example, when you’re on a business trip and you just show up at the dining table to eat and drink and you never see the bill, you probably don’t fret about the prices, right?

The key is to make your own money feel like somebody else’s, and you can do it like this:

Principle #3 – The Splurge Accountability Buddy

Many of us frugal people tend to stick together. And most of us have different versions of the same problem: we know logically that money is plentiful these days, but our emotions keep us stuck in our old ways of optimizing too much.

But I find that when I team up with local friends who are actually trying to battle these same habits, we can question each other’s decisions, call out cheapness when we see it, and cheer on splurges when we know the other guy would enjoy it.

My super wealthy friend from above has become much better about treating himself (and his family) to quality goods for the home, amazing trips together, and just a general reduction in his stress over being “efficient with money”

My friend and HQ co-owner Carl (Mr. 1500 Days) has finally replaced his beaten-down minivan with a spiffy new Chevrolet Bolt electric car, and is loving that leap into the future.

And of course Mr. Money Mustache, after squeezing one final mountain road trip out of his 23-year-old Honda van, is finally allowing himself to get the Tesla he has been talking about for half a decade.

A recent life change (becoming a co-owner of a fixer-upper vacation rental compound in beautiful Salida Colorado) has reignited the travel fire in my heart and made me realize how much I do love getting out to distant places for visiting, mountain biking, gathering with groups of friends and my favorite activity of all: Carpentourism.

Running the Numbers: how ridiculously expensive is this car?

This is the perfect start to my experiment in spending more. Realistically, a $50,000 car is going to cost me about $10,000 more per year than my old van was burning.  With the biggest costs being these:

Since I personally had a spending deficit of several times more than $10k per year, I figure this is a solid first step. And, since the car’s primary purpose is things like epic camping trips, dream dates, and  long adventures around the country, it will definitely help me spend more on experiences, hotels, and go out to dinner a bit more often as well.

“This Privileged Rich Folk Talk is Making Me Sick, why don’t you give your money away to charity, or to me?”

In general, I agree: the world has problems and the richer you are, the more you should consider giving generously.

But also, to be honest, the whiny people who constantly send complaints like this out to strangers on the Internet really need to get a life. It’s great to encourage philanthropy through positive examples, but completely unproductive to send negativity to shame people you don’t even know for not following your own personal value system. The world has seen more than enough of this.

On top of that, this one-sided thinking can be counterproductive. Both of my friends have given generously throughout their lifetimes. In my own case, I have donated over $500,000 to the best causes I could find during the years I’ve been writing this blog, but I was still refusing to let myself replace that 23-year-old van.

And that overthinking was leading to even more of a scarcity mentality, as I compared my own meager spending to these bigger numbers of my donations, and found myself thinking things like,

“Damn, I’m spending $100 on this dinner date which sounds like a lot, but I also spent ONE THOUSAND TIMES more on donations last year, which sounds like even more. Maybe I am spending too much and need to cut back on EVERYTHING!”And then the fear side of my brain would illogically chime in: “Yeah and you’re going to make us run out of money and be poor forever! waaaah waaaah! Cut back and optimize and conserve!”

Yes – be a super, duper responsible steward of your life savings.

And yes, give generously with all your heart to charity.

But yes, it’s also okay to set aside a portion of the money you’ve earned, for frivolous spending on yourself and those closest to you. You’re not a bad person for having a few nice things.

It’s okay to pay that extra hundred bucks to sit a bit closer to the front of the airplane instead of the back if it helps you enjoy your vacation and spend a joyful half hour walking FREE at your destination while the 49 rows of people behind you fuss infuriatingly with their shit in the overhead bins.

It’s okay to buy the frozen berries at Whole Foods even though they cost eight times more than Costco charges, if it spares you from making a second unpleasant trip through parking lot hell.

And as for me, I am calling it okay to, at last, double flip the Autopilot stalk in my new Tesla and lean back as it it shoots me gracefully through even the highest mountain passes, forever leaving the desperately underpowered wheezing and gear shifting and noise* of the gasoline era behind, forever.

I ended up using an online car salvage service called Peddle*, at the recommendation of a friend. With about five minutes of entering the details of my old Honda, their system offered me $715, and then a towtruck came and took it the next day – and actually gave me the payment in cash, which I found kind of fun. I made a point of using all of that money for splurges like dinners out, in keeping with the theme of this article.

* I later signed this blog up for Peddle’s affiliate program so that link will benefit MMM if you use it.

* A useful tip for more effective splurging:Try to find the truly negative aspects of your life and focus any additional spending on improving those things. But it’s a subtle art so you have to get it right if you want lasting results in happiness.

You don’t want to just reduce hardship or challenge like hiring someone to take care of every aspect of your house, because overcoming daily hardships and having significant accomplishments provides the very core of our life satisfaction.

You also don’t want to just upgrade the things that are already good in your life. For example, a friend of mine is a gourmet coffee expert, and he suggested that I upgrade my setup at home to include on-the-spot roasting, and fancy grinding and brewing equipment. But I already love the good quality coffee I buy off the shelf from Costco, so it would be counterproductive to invest time or money into changing this part of my life.

But when you have something that causes you regular angst and stress, whether it’s a leaky roof that makes you dread rain, or a long commute that makes you dread the daily traffic jam, or a body that is giving you trouble due to not being in the best of shape – those types of things are probably a good target for improvement.

In the case of my car situation, I had a Nissan Leaf which is wonderful to drive, but doesn’t have the range to travel anywhere outside of the Denver metro area. Then I had the van which is a clunky beast to drive, but is otherwise an amazing road tripper because I could bring along whatever and whoever I wanted. But the van was getting increasingly unreliable in several hard-to-fix ways which was making me nervous every time I thought about long distance travel. Which was causing me to avoid certain trips and miss positive lifetime experiences.

In other words, my lack of a reliable long-range car was a small but consistent source of negative stress.

Finally, Vanna gave me the gift of a final hot and smelly transmission failure on a mountain pass on the way home from my new project in Salida. It was just the nudge that I needed. And now I already feel excitement rather than dread at the prospect of all the road trips in the coming decades!

In that case, you might be interested in the Tesla Model 3 RWD, which uses only LFP – Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries (no cobalt and also no nickel). There are a few other advantages to this battery type as well, including even longer lifespan.

In the future, most cars will be using either LFP or Sodium-ion or other new chemistries based on even cheaper, more abundant minerals. I have a couple of points that come from what is glaringly obvious in your explanation of your purchases. The difference between someone who is a frugal saver and a spendthrift is that the frugal saver (I would put myself in this category) would not even consider the Dave’s bread at $7 and before buying the $4 bread would go look on the day old shelf for the same bread marked down to $2. The spendthrift ALWAYS buys this ONE treat, just this ONE time. The problem is, once the overpriced thing is bought, the thought of having overspent and treating ones self disappears from memory. Making this habit becomes the whole way of life for the spendthrift and come time to chuck the working life, the frugal guy says “Ok, let me do the math. Here’s my annual retirement budget and lot at this….I have 56 times this amount in liquid assets on my spread sheet inside my paid off house driven in by my paid off cars”. The spendthrift (who is actually a friend of Car Jack) looks and says “I have $100k in my 401k, rent and make payments on my car. How does anyone retire?”. So my advice is to check yourself each and every time you think about treating yourself. If you have the money and those treats keep you in the % spending, fine. If at the end of the year, you look at all that you spend and scream “Holy Shit….I spent what on this crap?”, you’ve failed to keep track of what you spend.

Ok, onto the Tesla. We all know you and many others have been very taken by the oversized electric golf carts. I went and drove a bunch of them myself in an effort to first find something I liked and then do the due diligence to justify a purchase. Do I sound like an engineer? Understandable with all the money I spent becoming one. In the end, I drove just about every EV, so I know the plusses and minuses of many of them. I will say that completely outside of the type of car, Elon has the absolute best way to buy a car. Go online, pick what you want, put in your deposit and wait till it’s ready. No listening to “What can I do to get you in a car today?” from some punk kid at a dealership. But in the end, I had to rely on math. What would it cost for ME to drive an EV of my choice. Well, I’d have to modify that to say the most efficient EV because to me the Audi e Tron GT was levels above every other EV I drove in luxury, quality and feeling more like a car with an electric drive system than an electric motor in tupperware. So the catch for me is that I live in a high electric rate area with wonderful total cost per kWh of 45.5 cents. And I’m seeing gas at the cheapo, competing gas stations for $2.89 per gallon on my way to the used tool store. My daily driver is a 2019 Subaru Crosstrek manual that gets 35 mpg in the summer. Note that ICE cars do worse in the winter because we have “winter gas” but also EVs do even more worse in winter temperatures. So in the end, a Tesla Model 3 single motor (the most efficient EV on the planet) calculates out to cost about 2 cents a mile MORE than my pedestrian Subaru that I bought new for $22k. So unless I’m looking to look like Richie Rich with a new Audi Electromobile, I can’t justify the thought of going electric. I’ll back up a second and admit that you people in like Texas who get electricity for 4 cents a kWh should absolutely look at EVs. But I don’t have that luxury. And gas is cheap here. And I like my car quite a lot with it’s utility, all wheel drive so I don’t have to trump up my driveway in the snow (it’s a steep hill that no 2 wheel drive can get up in snow) and I get fun from rowing gears. So my recommendation for anyone considering an EV is to DO THE MATH. the end.

Haha, yes I remember doing the same math when I saw that article! Although it looks like the Guardian has corrected the numbers in their article so it’s at least a bit less misleading.

It used to say that tires could emit over 9 grams of rubber dust per km of driving, and I calculated at the time the real number is 0.033 grams (33 milligrams) – because a tire loses about 2kg of mass over its 60,000 km lifespan. So, they were off by a factor of almost 300.

Now, they have fixed that to use a figure of 50 milligrams, which is close enough.

I don’t know how to calculate the amount that ends up in the air versus on the road, but either way, you have the same problem with electric cars or gas cars, and nowadays the weight is pretty similar across vehicle classes.

Then, there’s the fact that EVs almost never need their friction brakes, so brake dust is eliminated. And they don’t burn gas or oil, which results in cleaner air. Brilliant and balanced summary Jon, thanks for sharing it!

I often come back to the slogan “Everything is a Spectrum” – if you just label things as good or bad as the social media outrage world is prone to do, you miss out on the ability to make nuanced choices and really to make any progress on improving the world.

The best we can do is to make rough estimates of the NUMBERS behind each of our options, and then do tests and collect data so we can refine these numbers over time.

In other words, think of everything as a science experiment, and accept that you will always be somewhat wrong, but with sufficient humbleness and study you can gradually reduce this wrongness over time.

Space X created reusable rockets that can land vertically, greatly reducing the cost to NASA to resupply the International Space Station and freeing NASA from reliance on Russian rockets and transport. Based on what I’ve read about happiness, humans are generally terrible about figuring out what will make us happy. However, we’re actually very good at identifying things that are making us unhappy; also, unhappiness vs happiness is not a 1:1 comparison (more like 5:1, I believe).

Therefore, eliminating those things that make us unhappy is a logical, sensible and efficient strategy.

For many of us, jobs are the number one cause of dramatic unhappiness, because of the opportunity cost (i.e. time we could be spending on other things we value more), but also stress, commuting, and lack of freedom over our own destiny, etc. So FIRE is the first priority, because that has, by far, the most impact on happiness for most of us. (It’s not the only consideration though, because it takes years to achieve, so the journey matters a lot too).

Once that is achieved, the next steps are going to look very different for everyone, because everyone is different. Many for someone, that’s cutting their own lawn, so they hire someone. For someone else, they hate baking bread, so they buy it pre-made.

Around my house, we refer to it as, “throwing money at the problem”. I detest working on cars, so I always take them to our trusted mechanic. However, I like (or at least don’t mind) carpentry, plumbing, electrical, etc, so I do almost all of that work myself.

MMM identified something that was negatively impacting his level of happiness/life satisfaction, determined the cost to fix it (vs doing other things with that money, because everything is balancing cost/benefit), and decided that the tradeoffs were worth it. It was a decision he researched thoroughly, and although it might not be perfectly logical (although it’s entirely possible it is), he even understood the emotional factors contributing to the decision – we’re humans, not Vulcans! It didn’t impact his life in a negative way financially or otherwise, it doesn’t disproportionately hurt the earth (given the society he lives in), and most importantly, he didn’t make the consumerist mistake of believing that buying the Tesla would make him happy.

That’s the root of the problem for most people, I think – they are constantly fed advertising that convinces them that spending money on something will make them happy. It won’t EVER do that, but using it to remove frustration and pain from your life can definitely improve our level of happiness.

It’s tricky and complicated figuring out that balance at times for sure, but everything is always a balance. Almost nothing in life is binary.

Charging in our Y is definitely way less convenient in multi supercharger distance trips than in a gas car. 20K miles of road trips so far. The key is MULTI. A distance of just one supercharger is fine. The problem is you trickle charge when above 80% full.

Charge-discharge cycles using 30% (100 miles), instead of 100% (300+ miles), changes that 1,000 cycle life into 15,000 cycle life. Also remember that after 300,000 miles, the battery doesn’t die outright! Now it will simply hold 253 miles instead of 316 miles. Still very usable, and nowhere near dead; it’ll hold up for 1,000,000 miles no problem.

Electrek reports that the oldest vehicles, Model S and X, have 10-15% range loss after 200,000 miles. I can personally verify this: My 2014 Model S had a range of 265 miles from the factory. Now I have 275,000 miles on it, and my range is 243 miles, a mere 8.4% loss.

There are Tesla Model S with much older designed packs still on the road from 2015 and 80-90% capacity which is more than sufficient. Battery degradation will not be an issue. Other components might fail before the battery does, depending on the climate he uses it in

#8690. Why the Spanish Squat Can Help Build Quads without Using a Barbell

The traditional back squat has long been the staple of those who want to crush their quads, but standing under a heavy barbell is not for everyone. Mature gym goers, or anyone with mobility issues, may find that the downward force of carrying a heavy bar across the shoulders leads to stress on the spine. Fortunately, IFBB Pro and physique transformation coach, Tanya Johansen swears by the Spanish squat.

“Try a Spanish squat,” recommends the Bikini Pro competitor. “It fries your quads… when done correctly.”

The Spanish squat is a popular movement utilized for rehabbing the knees, but it also pounds the quadriceps, providing the perfect environment for muscle growth. To try it for yourself, stand in front of a cable station or power rack and anchor a resistance band around the support, looping around the back of your knees. You can stand inside a single loop, or loop the band around each knee, as demonstrated by Johansen.

Next, move back a little to make sure there is tension on the band. Now, you should be able to squat by sitting back with the band keeping you upright. Keep your shins vertical, and place emphasis on the quads as you lift and lower your body.  “Band behind your knees, sit back into it, stay tall, let your knees come forward,” summarized the coach, who specializes in physiques that are over 40.

Because there is no barbell compressing your body, the Spanish squat can be executed without overloading the back and knee joints. The quads can still be worked hard with no additional weight, and for those looking to improve their range of mobility, Spanish squats are awesome for building knee strength because they rehab the patellar and its related tendons.

“Over 40? Even better reason,” advises the coach of the Spanish squat. “You don’t need a heavy bar on your back to grow your legs. Forget heavy. Make the muscle do the work.”  And, for those who use the barbell as a crux for their ego, this IFBB Pro has some real talk. “You’re not in there to impress anyone,” she explained. “You’re in there to make sure your quads earn it.”

To make this move more challenging, you can bring in an isometric hold at the top of the squat, pausing before descending back down. You can also slow down the lowering phase for additional time under tension. Aim for 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

“It’s not the weight. It’s the work,” concluded Johansen, who’s own physique is proof positive that training smart can bring serious progress.
